pll1d11c1-d1e3477.summary: States the thesis of the distinction: the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son and proceeds from both, which many heretics have denied.
claims: The Holy Spirit proceeds from both the Father and the Son.

pll1d11c1-d1e3480.summary: Announces that procession from both is proved by many scriptural testimonies.

pll1d11c1-d1e3489.summary: Cites Galatians 4:6 ('the Spirit of his Son') and Romans 8:9 ('the Spirit of Christ') as calling the Spirit the Spirit of the Son.
claims: Scripture calls the Holy Spirit the Spirit of the Son.

pll1d11c1-d1e3514.summary: Adds texts showing that the Son sends the Spirit from the Father (John 15:26) and that the Spirit is the Father's (Rom 8:11; Matt 10:20), sent by the Father in the Son's name, and proceeding from the Father (John 14:26; 15:26).
claims: The Son sends the Spirit from the Father.
The Spirit is called the Spirit of the Father and proceeds from the Father.

pll1d11c1-d1e3565.summary: Concludes from these authorities that the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son.
claims: The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

pll1d11c1-d1e3568.summary: Reports that the Greeks say the Spirit proceeds only from the Father, not from the Son.
claims: The Greeks hold procession from the Father alone.

pll1d11c1-d1e3580.summary: Gives the Greek reasons: in the Gospel, which contains the whole faith, Christ names only the Father; and the creeds of the principal councils held in the East, sealed with anathemas against teaching otherwise, mention procession from the Father only. So the Greeks hold that anyone adding 'from the Son' is anathema, and accuse the Latins.
claims: The Gospel names only the Father in speaking of procession.
The conciliar creeds forbid teaching otherwise than they contain.
The Greeks consider the Latins anathematized.

pll1d11c1-d1e3592.summary: Adds the Greeks' appeal to the creed that Leo III had engraved on a silver tablet behind the altar of St Paul in Rome, which says the Spirit proceeds 'from the Father.' This is the creed sung at Mass, with its closing anathema, so they say the Latin addition 'Filioque' incurs it.
claims: Leo III's tablet of the creed has procession from the Father only.
The Latins added 'Filioque' to the creed.

pll1d11c1-d1e3624.summary: Lombard's reply: 'whoever teaches otherwise' means teaching the contrary, as in Paul's 'if anyone preach another gospel' (Gal 1:8). Paul did not forbid adding, since, as Augustine notes, he himself wished to supply what was lacking to the Thessalonians' faith. Supplying adds what was lacking without removing what was there; departing from the rule of faith is leaving the way.
claims: The anathema condemns contrary teaching, not addition.
Adding what is lacking is not departing from the faith.
Departing from the rule of faith is what is condemned.

pll1d11c1-d1e3675.summary: Answers the Gospel argument: Christ says the Spirit proceeds from the Father but not 'from the Father alone,' so he does not deny procession from himself. He names the Father because he usually refers to him even what is his own, since he has it from him.
claims: John 15:26 does not say 'from the Father alone.'
The Son refers to the Father what is his own because he has it from the Father.

pl-l1d11c1.summary: Asserts against heretics that the Holy Spirit is from and proceeds from both Father and Son, citing Scripture that calls him the Spirit of the Son and of the Father and says both send him. Lombard sets out the Greek position that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone: Christ names only the Father in John 15:26, and the anathemas of the councils forbid teaching 'otherwise' than the Creed, which Leo III had inscribed without the Filioque, so the Greeks call the Latins anathematized for the addition. Lombard answers that 'teaching otherwise' means teaching the contrary, not adding, as Augustine shows from Galatians 1:8. In John 15:26 Christ does not say 'from the Father alone,' and names the Father because he refers to the Father what is his own.
claims: The Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son and proceeds from both.
Scripture calls the Spirit both the Spirit of the Son and of the Father, and says both send him.
The Greeks hold that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone.
The conciliar anathema against teaching 'otherwise' condemns teaching the contrary, not supplementing.
Christ's naming only the Father in John 15:26 does not exclude procession from the Son.
